claims.text: The initial TiVNbTa alloy is an as-cast, single-phase BCC material.
The baseline TiVNbTa alloy has a yield strength of approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
The baseline TiVNbTa alloy has approximately 40% ductility.
The baseline TiVNbTa alloy has inadequate high-temperature strength retention for reliable divertor service.
Annealing TiVNbTa at approximately 1000 °C for a short duration will homogenize its microstructure.
Aging the annealed TiVNbTa alloy at 800–900 °C will produce fine, dispersed Ti-rich or Nb-rich nanoscale precipitates.
A controlled atmosphere during thermal treatment will prevent oxidation and maintain alloy purity.
The induced nanoscale precipitates will remain dispersed within the BCC matrix.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede dislocation glide.
Precipitation strengthening will increase high-temperature yield strength and compressive strength.
The treated alloy will have yield and compressive strengths above approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
The treated alloy will retain approximately 40% ductility.
The precipitation treatment will not significantly compromise TiVNbTa thermal conductivity.
Preserving thermal conductivity will allow efficient heat transfer between W and CuCrZr.
The predicted enhancement is effective within an aging range of 800–900 °C and during testing at 1273 K up to 30% strain.
Departures from the specified processing conditions may alter precipitate formation, precipitate stability, and performance.
The treatment will improve TiVNbTa performance as an intermediate layer between W and CuCrZr.

contradictions.description: Testing only up to 30% strain cannot establish the prediction that approximately 40% ductility or strain to failure is maintained.

The prediction treats approximately 330 MPa as the comparison level for both yield and compressive strength, whereas the baseline field identifies 330 MPa only as yield strength and provides no compressive-strength baseline.

The rule states that any strength, precipitate, ductility, or conductivity failure falsifies both the performance prediction and precipitation-hardening mechanism. These are separable claims: for example, reduced conductivity would not by itself falsify precipitation strengthening, and absent precipitates would not by itself prove that the strength prediction failed.
